doc.title: Gerald Wiggins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 2, 1995

title: On the road with Spike Jones
summary: He filled in for Arnold Ross, found the music hard and precisely timed, and recalls Spike's humor and band members.

bands.name: Spike Jones and His City Slickers

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: I think I read you worked with Spike Jones?

Yeah well, that happened, that’s right. I was working with Spike’s wife, Helen Grayco. And Spike’s piano player Arnold Ross became ill, so Spike asked Helen could he borrow me for a while. So I went on the road with the Spike Jones band. And that was a trip. I said this crazy music, this ought to be fun to play. I think the first tune was “Poet and Peasant” for real. You know so if you couldn’t read you were in a whole lot of trouble. Fortunately I could read. That was tough music.
Yeah, you had to be good to play in that.

And everything was timed to the second. And there was no goofing on that gig, believe me. Spike was a funny man but he was a taskmaster too, you know, you had to do it. I remember the first time I went to his home I walked in and there was a picture of the Blue Boy with Spike’s head on top of it, which cracked me up. But then the next picture was Whistler’s Mother with a racing form in her lap. And that was Spike all the way. He used to go to all the dog kennels when we were traveling, and tape the dogs barking and everything, and they put a record together of “Memories are Made of Things Like This” or something. He put all those dogs barking and this tune was fantastic.
Oh he was something else, he was fantastic, yeah, I really loved him.
And we listen to that stuff now and we remember that it was done without any studio tricks, just live.
Oh yeah, that was just him editing and putting it together.
That’s interesting. They had some hot players though, to pull that stuff off.

Oh, yeah. He had George Rock who was a fantastic trumpet player. And the tenor player Gil Bernal, he’s still around. He called me a couple of years ago, he’s been on the same job out here for about 30 years. I’d wondered what happened to him, you know. And there was Mousey, and oh what was the little midget’s name?
Oh, I remember from the T.V. shows they did, that guy running out on stage, the real small one.
Yeah. Billy Barty. Yeah he was there. Yeah, Spike had quite a show.
In what kind of venue — where would you play with him? In what kind of setting?
Oh we did all the college gyms.
Yeah. In the middle of winter. And it was something else. It wasn’t bad. I had a lot of fun.
